data.title: Traditional Jazan Woven-Rope Daybed Craft Preserves Heritage, Earns International Design Recognition
data.content:
Jizan, November 20, 2026, SPA -- Traditional furniture from Jazan Region preserves intricate craftsmanship, demonstrating human ingenuity in adapting local environmental resources into durable, aesthetically appealing pieces.
    Among the most iconic examples is the traditional woven-rope daybed, historically placed prominently inside traditional conical huts for special occasions, with smaller versions used for daily gatherings.
    Inspired by this craft, artisans at the Artisans House in Jazan created a decorative craft mural that won a Silver Award at the 2025 New York Product Design Awards, as announced by the Heritage Commission on December 14, 2025.
    Crafting the daybed begins with constructing a rectangular frame—measuring roughly two meters long, one meter wide, and standing 75 centimeters high on four corner posts—typically using local jujube wood. The carpenter smooths and curves the side and end rails to minimize friction before fitting them into carved mortises to form a stable base. A specialized weaver then stretches twisted palm-frond ropes across the frame in sequential rows, using simple tools and practiced skill to gauge tension and maintain uniform spacing. Finally, women attach a woven palm-frond mat over the surface to protect the ropes from wear and complete the piece, which is produced in various sizes as well as a chair-like variant with a wooden backrest.
    To pass these traditional skills to new generations amid changing lifestyles, the Heritage Commission included woven daybed production in a year-long training program at the Artisans House in Jazan, alongside traditional cap weaving and seashell crafts. The program trained 30 artisans in technical craftsmanship, innovation, design, entrepreneurship, and marketing, encouraging them to integrate geometric patterns and modern color palettes into natural materials to suit contemporary market demands while preserving core crafting methods.
    During a ceremony at the Prince Sultan Cultural Center in Jazan on February 13, 2026, the Heritage Commission announced that the number of licensed artisans in the region had surpassed 270 and that the Artisans House had produced over 2,000 handcrafted items, honoring the artisans behind the award-winning mural for transforming inherited knowledge into an internationally acclaimed work.
    -- SPA
